Perplexed
per-PLEXT
v. (past part.) and adj.
From Latin perplexus, entangled, intricate, from per (thoroughly) and plectere (to weave, to braid). Webster 1828: made intricate; puzzled; embarrassed with doubt. The root image is a knot — threads woven together past the point of untangling.

Biblical Definition

Perplexed is the state of a man who cannot see his way through, and Paul’s use of it is one of the most precise sentences in the New Testament about Christian suffering: We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair (2 Corinthians 4:8). He concedes the perplexity outright. The apostle does not claim to understand what God is doing; he claims only that being at a loss is not the same as being without hope, and the Greek makes a deliberate play — at a loss, but not utterly at a loss. The word is used of a king who cannot make sense of a report: Now Herod the tetrarch heard of all that was done by him: and he was perplexed, because that it was said of some, that John was risen from the dead (Luke 9:7). It is used of a whole city under an incomprehensible decree, in one of Scripture’s most chilling contrasts: the king and Haman sat down to drink; but the city Shushan was perplexed (Esther 3:15). And Joel uses it of animals in a famine, which is oddly moving: How do the beasts groan! the herds of cattle are perplexed, because they have no pasture (Joel 1:18).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines PERPLEXED as made intricate or involved; entangled; puzzled; embarrassed with doubt or difficulty; rendered unable to decide or to see the way forward.

expand to see more

PERPLEXED, pp. — Made intricate; entangled; involved so that the parts cannot be readily distinguished.

Puzzled; embarrassed with doubt; unable to determine what to think or to do.

Harassed with anxiety or vexation arising from uncertainty.

Applied to affairs, questions, and paths, as well as to persons.

From Latin per, thoroughly, and plecto, to weave — the root also of complex, plait, and pleat.

Key Scripture

2 Corinthians 4:8 — "We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair;"

Luke 9:7 — "Now Herod the tetrarch heard of all that was done by him: and he was perplexed, because that it was said of some, that John was risen from the dead;"

Esther 3:15 — "The posts went out, being hastened by the king's commandment, and the decree was given in Shushan the palace. And the king and Haman sat down to drink; but the city Shushan was perplexed."

Joel 1:18 — "How do the beasts groan! the herds of cattle are perplexed, because they have no pasture; yea, the flocks of sheep are made desolate."

Modern Corruption

Both the triumphalist teaching that a believer walking rightly always understands what God is doing, and the counsel that unresolved bewilderment is grounds for abandoning faith, are refused by a single clause: perplexed, but not in despair.

expand to see more

Paul’s four contrasts in 2 Corinthians 4:8-9 are all built the same way — troubled but not distressed, perplexed but not in despair, persecuted but not forsaken, cast down but not destroyed. In every pair the first term is granted in full. He is genuinely at a loss. Against the prosperity and victorious-life teachings, which treat confusion as a symptom of insufficient faith, Paul places bewilderment among the ordinary conditions of apostolic ministry and never suggests it should be resolved before the work continues. The believer is not promised comprehension. He is promised that the treasure is in earthen vessels that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us.

The opposite corruption treats the same experience as a verdict. Where a person has been taught that faith means understanding, a season of genuine perplexity presents itself as evidence that the whole thing was false, and the modern deconstruction narrative usually runs through exactly this point. Paul’s distinction is the answer, and it is a real distinction rather than a word game: to be at a loss for the meaning of a providence is one thing; to conclude there is no meaning is another, and nothing compels the second from the first. Esther 3:15 shows what such a moment looks like from the outside — the decree published, the city bewildered, the king drinking — and the book’s whole point is that God’s hand was in it although His name is never mentioned.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek aporeo (G639), to be without a way, to be at a loss; exaporeomai (G1820), to be utterly without a way, to despair; Hebrew bok (H943), to be confused, entangled.

expand to see more

Greek aporeo (G639) — to be without passage, at a loss; from a-, not, and poros, a way through.

Greek exaporeomai (G1820) — to be utterly at a loss, to despair; Paul’s deliberate contrast in 2 Corinthians 4:8.

Hebrew bok (H943) — to be confounded, entangled; They are entangled in the land (Exodus 14:3).

Greek diaporeo (G1280) — to be thoroughly perplexed; Herod in Luke 9:7 and the crowd at Pentecost (Acts 2:12).

Greek thlibo (G2346) — to press, to afflict; the troubled on every side of the same verse.

Usage

"We are perplexed, but not in despair (2 Corinthians 4:8) — the loss granted in full, the conclusion refused."

"The king and Haman sat down to drink; but the city Shushan was perplexed (Esther 3:15) — bewilderment seen from outside."

"The herds of cattle are perplexed, because they have no pasture (Joel 1:18) — even the beasts under a judgment they cannot read."
